candidateRows: The deductive moral argument is unnecessarily brittle and conceptually underdetermined, so the moral case should instead be framed abductively.
This critique motivates the shift from a familiar deductive moral argument to the abductive framework governing the entire discussion.
After presenting the standard deductive argument, David questions its counterfactual premise, its conception of objectivity, and its vulnerability to a single defeated premise.
Theism should be compared with secular ethical theories as an explanation of moral facts, knowledge, transformation, and rationality using standard explanatory criteria.
This is the affirmative's governing argument: the four moral phenomena are evidence to be explained by comparing theistic and secular candidates.

David defines inference to the best explanation, identifies four classes of moral phenomena, proposes comparative explanatory criteria, and emphasizes that the result supplies plausibility rather than certainty.
The abductive case has not justified either the moral phenomena needing explanation or God as a reasonable candidate explanation.
The objection attacks both inputs of the affirmative inference: the purported explanatory data and the eligibility of the proposed theistic explanation.
David's proposed abductive comparison of theistic and secular explanations for the fourfold moral evidence.

Matt accepts abduction generally but argues that candidate explanations require independent justification, questions whether a god is possible, and says observed morality may already have an adequate explanation.
The moral evidence comprises objective values and duties, moral knowledge, moral transformation, and a rational congruence between morality and human fulfillment.
These definitions specify the explananda on which the affirmative's comparative theistic case depends and establish the scope of the motion-level claim.
Matt's contention that the purported moral phenomena were insufficiently specified and might not require further explanation.

David clarifies that moral facts mean objective values and duties, distinguishes epistemic knowledge and personal transformation, and defines rationality through harmony between moral life and fulfillment.
Plausible explanatory candidates emerge from careful examination of the evidence, and the potential explanatory power of theism warrants keeping it under consideration.
This directly defends the disputed admission of theism into the candidate set, without which the proposed abductive comparison could not proceed.
Matt's objection that God lacks demonstrated justification for admission as a candidate in an abductive inference.
David denies that candidate selection follows an airtight algorithm, connects it to close study of the evidence, and argues against excluding theistic explanations at the outset.
Although abduction yields less certainty, a modest conclusion can make the overall argument stronger, and this moral argument need only contribute to a cumulative theistic case.
The move defines the intended epistemic strength and cumulative role of the affirmative case, answering a central objection about abductive weakness and ambition.
Matt's claim that abduction is the weakest inference form and unsuitable for establishing a question as important as God's existence.
David distinguishes a weaker conclusion from a weaker argument, says restrained conclusions demand less from their premises, and places the moral argument within a larger cumulative inquiry.
Treating God as a viable explanation while using the argument to establish God risks circularity unless God's candidacy receives prior independent justification.
This sharpens the principal challenge to the affirmative methodology by arguing that the conclusion cannot be presupposed as an eligible explanatory candidate.
David's characterization of Matt as having an a priori resistance to including theism among possible explanations.

Matt says he resists every candidate until its eligibility is demonstrated, distinguishes that standard from excluding theism in advance, and warns that presuming God's viability may beg the question.
Moral transformation occurs through secular natural processes, while belief in a supervising deity could motivate change even if the belief were false.
The move supplies a direct secular rival explanation for one of the affirmative's four major explananda and challenges its claimed evidential preference for theism.
David's inclusion of moral transformation among the phenomena purportedly better explained by a theistic account.
Matt notes that people improve without religion and argues that ordinary learning, incentives, punishment, parenthood, or even a useful false belief can produce behavioral transformation.
Even the best available explanation should not be inferred as probably true when intrinsically unlikely, so the moral case at most supplies some reason for theism within total evidence.
This establishes the affirmative's bounded conclusion and an internal safeguard on abductive inference, determining exactly what success on the motion would support.
Matt's objection that calling God the best explanation for morality remains an ambitious conclusion despite the argument's abductive form.

David explains that relative explanatory superiority does not overcome low intrinsic probability and concludes that morality could provide limited evidence for God even if the total evidence supports atheism.
An accurate account of morality need not provide rational support for God because moral intuitions and practices can arise through parental teaching and shared culture.
This rejects even the affirmative's modest evidential conclusion and begins offering a secular account of why morality can seem innate or author-dependent.
David's modest conclusion that morality, under the proposed understanding, can supply some reason to believe that God exists.
Matt grants that people can move from moral experience to belief in a moral author but calls that inference flawed and points toward learning and cultural transmission instead.
The relevant theistic conception is the omnipotent, omniscient, and morally perfect God of classical theism rather than an initially Christian-specific conception.
Specifying the proposed explanatory entity is necessary to assess whether theism supplies a coherent and superior explanation of moral facts.
Dillahunty's objection that the discussion had not defined God or established access to that God's moral character.
After Dillahunty questions both the identity of the proposed God and the reliability of biblical moral claims, Baggett identifies classical theism as his operative starting point.
The moral-transformation component concerns whether secular naturalism can sustain a realistic hope for complete moral transformation, not whether ordinary improvement is possible.
The proposition states one of the expressly identified explanatory dimensions on which theism and secular accounts are being compared.
Before turning to objective values and duties, Baggett clarifies the scope of his less-emphasized moral-transformation argument and its intended contrast with secular naturalism.
Objective moral values are intrinsically good, while objective duties are binding, authoritative, and sometimes categorical prescriptions admitting no exception.
These definitions establish the central moral phenomena whose existence and explanatory significance the debate's competing worldviews must address.
At the start of the objectivity discussion, Baggett defines intrinsic moral value and authoritative obligation, illustrating categorical duty with gratuitous child torture.
Moral obligations appear objectively authoritative and universally binding, while guilt after violating them is evidence that calls for an explanation of moral authority.
The move identifies the central evidence for objective obligation and frames its authoritative and guilt-producing character as explananda favoring a deeper account.
Dillahunty's contention that adding motivation and context to an act does not establish a moral absolute in the relevant sense.
Baggett treats the semantic disagreement about absolutes as minor, then argues that binding obligations present as facts independent of preference and generate fitting guilt when violated.
Guilt is culturally variable and cannot ground objective morality; objective assessments instead concern how actions affect adopted goals such as survival and well-being.
This supplies a secular account of moral evaluation while directly challenging a principal phenomenon offered as evidence for authoritative objective obligations.
Baggett's claim that guilt phenomenology indicates objective, universally binding moral obligations requiring explanation.

Dillahunty cites people who do not share the same guilt responses, distinguishes chosen foundational goals from objective means-end facts, and argues that harm can remain wrong without guilt or divine commands.
Guilt was offered only as evidence of moral authority, and its phenomenology can reasonably indicate genuine wrongdoing rather than merely cultural conditioning.
The response protects a principal evidential premise from the objection that variability and socialization render guilt wholly subjective and explanatorily irrelevant.
Dillahunty's argument that guilt is subjective, culturally imposed, and unnecessary for judging conduct wrong.
Baggett denies resting the entire case on guilt, contrasts conventions with potentially necessary moral truths, and argues that remorse often presents as deserved recognition of actual wrongdoing.
Empathy and role reversal explain conscience and much apparent moral authority without requiring religious commands or any further supernatural foundation.
The move proposes a secular psychological and deliberative mechanism for moral judgment, directly competing with the claim that perceived authority requires theism.
Baggett's defense of guilt as reasonable evidence that people apprehend objective moral wrongdoing rather than mere social conditioning.
Dillahunty locates guilt in empathy, recommends assessing actions through universalization and role reversal, and treats conscience as explicable without divine conviction.
Empathy cannot ground moral obligation because cultivating and exercising empathy is itself something people are morally obligated to do and therefore still needs a foundation.
This is a regress-style challenge to the proposed secular foundation: the mechanism offered to explain obligation already presupposes an authoritative obligation.
Dillahunty's claim that empathy and role reversal sufficiently explain conscience and perceived moral authority.
Baggett accepts empathy's importance but argues that the duty to cultivate it means empathy is an object of obligation rather than the source of authoritative moral law.
Some foundational moral principles can be rationally accepted as obvious, properly basic axioms from which ethical reasoning proceeds even though their truth is not thereby proven.
The move supplies Baggett's epistemology of moral knowledge and explains how basic moral principles can be warranted without inferential proof.
Dillahunty's demand for an authoritative foundation explaining why people morally should care about others' well-being.
In response to the demand for a further argument, Baggett treats concern for others and the wrongness of gratuitous torture as exceptionally obvious starting points from which one reasons.
Human-benefiting moral axioms can generate coherent ethical systems and arise similarly under godless physical conditions, so their axiomatic status does not require God as an explanation.
The move offers a secular origin and justification for foundational moral commitments while directly denying the inference from their apparent basicness to God.
Baggett's proposal that obvious foundational moral principles may be accepted as properly basic axiomatic starting points.
Dillahunty argues that life, health, and pleasure can be adopted as axioms, that contrary axioms self-defeat, and that similar creatures would converge because of shared physical needs.
Some moral obligations are categorical requirements that cannot be reduced to instrumental reasoning about achieving chosen goals.
The distinction between categorical and instrumental requirements supplies the kind of authoritative moral fact that his theistic explanation is designed to explain.
Dillahunty's account derives practical conclusions from a prior commitment to well-being and its associated goals.
After distinguishing epistemic justification from ontological explanation, Baggett argues that goal-directed practical reasoning does not capture every genuine moral obligation.
Once concern for well-being is adopted, actions can be evaluated by their effects without introducing additional categorical oughts.
This move directly contests the claimed need for irreducible categorical obligations and extends a well-being account to difficult cases involving the dead and animals.
Baggett's claim that some acts remain categorically forbidden even when they produce no wider harmful consequences.
Dillahunty concedes that the initial commitment to well-being is not derived, but argues that subsequent judgments concern movement toward or away from that goal.
A morality confined to human flourishing is too narrow because animal suffering and the formation of moral character also matter intrinsically.
The move tests the scope of Dillahunty's flourishing standard and restores moral transformation as an independently important dimension of the broader moral case.
Dillahunty's suggestion that concern for animals can be grounded primarily in effects on people and on the torturer's psyche.
Baggett argues that torturing even an unowned wild animal seems wrong and adds that morality evaluates the kinds of persons our repeated choices make us.
Binding, objective, prescriptive moral obligations call for explanation, and a loving creator provides a stronger account of their authority.
This is the chunk's fullest statement of the core inference from authoritative moral obligation to theism as a comparatively strong explanatory hypothesis.
Dillahunty's secular account treats moral objectivity and obligation through well-being without an externally authoritative moral law.
Baggett identifies authoritative obligation as the relevant datum, says rival accounts must be compared abductively, and proposes a loving creator who equips humans to apprehend moral truth.
Methodological naturalism permits demonstrated supernatural causes but rejects an unexplained deity that adds mystery without predictive or explanatory power.
The response attacks both the alleged exclusion of theism in advance and the explanatory adequacy of God while offering plausible natural mechanisms and epistemic restraint.
Baggett's contention that methodological naturalism stacks the deck against evidence whose proper explanation may transcend nature.
Dillahunty distinguishes methodological from philosophical naturalism, warns that unconstrained supernatural hypotheses proliferate, and favors natural models or suspended judgment absent evidence.
A flourishing-based account fails to capture the categorical authority and guilt involved in paradigmatic atrocities such as the Holocaust.
The reply defends the distinctive moral datum required by Baggett's argument by claiming that secular goal-directed language understates atrocity's authoritative wrongness.
Dillahunty's naturalistic explanation of moral feelings and his claim that well-being supplies an adequate objective evaluative standard.
Baggett grants that both views reject subjectivism but argues that only his stronger conception includes moral law, categorical requirements, and genuine guilt for violations.
Positing God as morality's foundation does not solve moral disagreement unless people can reliably identify the good deity and access its requirements.
The move challenges theism's explanatory usefulness by arguing that divine grounding yields further unresolved epistemic and Euthyphro-style problems rather than practical moral access.
Baggett's claim that an authoritative moral law and categorical condemnation of atrocities are better explained by God.
Dillahunty provisionally grants a classical-theist foundation, then asks what follows without dependable access, noting that opposing agents have claimed divine authorization.
Theistic ethics requires a morally perfect, maximally great God, and moral considerations can distinguish that hypothesis from finite or capricious deities.
The reply clarifies that the explanatory hypothesis is not an arbitrary god and claims that moral evidence helps narrow natural theology toward a maximally good being.
Dillahunty's objection that believers cannot establish which alleged deity is good or distinguish divine goodness from imposed conditioning.
Baggett denies that every conception of God can ground ethics, invokes the omni-attributes, and contrasts a maximally great being with fallible deities subject to humanlike failings.
Taking categorical moral authority seriously makes morality evidentially significant and supports God as an explanation of an authoritative moral law.
This move directly links categorical obligation, moral law, and ultimate reality, thereby restating the debate's principal pro-theistic inference in compact form.
Dillahunty's objection that defining an all-good God makes the explanation tautological and supplies no reason to believe such a being exists.
Baggett says a robust view of atrocity's intrinsic wrongness indicates an authoritative moral law whose existence needs explanation and may therefore provide reason for theism.
Moral intuitions can motivate investigation of reality, but they do not establish God and theistic explanations may obstruct further inquiry.
The response grants an epistemic role for moral experience while denying the crucial inference to theism and alleging that premature divine explanations hinder discovery.
Baggett's claim that authoritative moral intuitions reveal features of ultimate reality and provide evidential support for God's existence.
Dillahunty allows that unexplained intuitions prompt inquiry, attributes perceived authority partly to prescriptive social upbringing, and denies that this inquiry has moved closer to God.
Confidence in an abductive conclusion should be limited by the quality and depth of the available pool of explanations.
The move supplies a general epistemic constraint on the abductive method used to support the theistic moral explanation.
The bad-lot objection that a best available explanation may come from an inadequate candidate pool.
After the moderator introduces the bad-lot objection, Dillahunty connects it to his earlier concern about selecting candidates and recommends proportioning confidence to the adequacy of the pool.
The bad-lot objection can be accommodated by treating the moral argument as providing only a qualified increase in the plausibility of theism.
This move directly limits the intended force of the abductive moral argument while preserving its relevance as comparative support for theism.
The objection that superiority within a possibly bad explanatory pool cannot justify believing the winning explanation true.

Following Dillahunty's proposed confidence constraint, Baggett concedes that comparative victory need not warrant belief in theism and reframes the result as a potentially marginal, morality-specific likelihood increase.
A theistic explanation could outperform individual secular alternatives without defeating every combination of them, and prior skepticism can independently derail the inference.
The move identifies two further limits on what comparative explanatory success can establish, clarifying the argument's acknowledged scope and dependence on priors.
The bad-lot challenge to moving from comparative explanatory advantage to a warranted conclusion that theism is true.

Baggett continues his concessions by distinguishing individual alternatives from combinations and by acknowledging that sufficiently low prior confidence in theism may prevent the argument from persuading.
The moral argument is best understood as one component of a cumulative case, yielding moral reasons for theism rather than a standalone conclusion.
This move states the pro side's ultimate claimed explanatory payoff and locates it within a broader case rather than presenting it as a decisive proof.
The concern that acknowledged abductive limitations prevent the moral argument from rationally supporting theism at all.

After listing concessions to the bad-lot problem, Baggett says the argument works best alongside other arguments and can provide moral reasons for belief even when it does not settle one's final worldview.
God should not enter the pool of candidate moral explanations until the claimed divine being has been demonstrated to be a possible explanation.
The move challenges the admissibility of theism in the central abductive comparison, potentially blocking the explanatory inference before relative merits are considered.
Baggett's use of classical theism as a candidate explanation for multiple facets of morality.
In his closing remarks, Dillahunty acknowledges that Baggett is not offering a knockdown proof but argues that an unknown God's mere description does not yet qualify it as an available explanation.
Persistent divine hiddenness is morally unexpected if a good creator could clarify a harmful, consequential dispute about that creator's existence.
The move presents a morally grounded expectation that counts against the proposed divine explanation and directly links divine character to observable nonintervention.
The claim that a morally perfect creator is a plausible explanatory basis for objective morality and moral obligations.

Dillahunty argues that a good creator should intervene when prolonged uncertainty causes social harm or alleged damnation, especially if humans otherwise reach plausible but mistaken natural explanations.
Moral experience provides no perceived need for a nonnatural explanation and supplies reasons not to make the inferential leap to one.
The move gives the con side's bottom-line answer to the debate's explanatory comparison by denying both the need and justification for a nonnatural posit.
Baggett's overall contention that features of morality call for a classical-theistic explanation.
After presenting the hiddenness objection, Dillahunty closes by saying his understanding of morality discloses neither a nonnatural explanation nor a reason to move beyond natural accounts.
A worldview may fairly be compared for its explanatory power without first being independently established as true or possible by a separate argument.
The move defends including theism in the abductive comparison by applying the same methodological permission that would be granted to a naturalistic explanation.
Dillahunty's claim that God cannot be used as a candidate explanation until divine possibility is first demonstrated.

Baggett tests Dillahunty's restriction by considering a naturalist who proposes that naturalism explains morality, arguing that he would regard that explanatory proposal as fair game without prior establishment.
Divine hiddenness may serve priorities beyond producing bare belief in God's existence, because relationship requires more than mere recognition that someone exists.
The move offers an alternative account of why a good God might remain partly hidden, answering a major consideration Dillahunty presented against theism.
Dillahunty's argument that a good creator would reveal itself clearly enough to resolve harmful religious disagreement.

Baggett concedes that universal bare belief could be produced by obvious manifestation but suggests that God may have other relational priorities, illustrated by the difference between believing in a spouse and having a relationship.
A reductive naturalistic account of morality inadequately captures the human condition and the phenomenology of moral experience.
The move returns to the core explanatory comparison by asserting that the secular account fails to preserve important features of morality as humans experience it.
Dillahunty's naturalistic understanding of morality and denial that moral phenomena require a nonnatural explanation.

Baggett says their principal disagreement concerns what moral phenomena require by way of explanation, then judges the opposing account too deflationary and reductionist to fit lived moral experience.
